headline: Planes, trains and automobiles: The best ways to beat travel fatigue—so you can come home feeling rested and fulfilled
author: Renée Onque

paragraphs.text: Five-hour flights. Eleven-hour road trips. Fifteen-hour train rides. All potentially exhausting options for the annual tradition of convening around the dinner table with loved ones on Thanksgiving.

An estimated 81.5 million Americans are projected to travel, or have already traveled, at least 50 miles from their homes between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30, according to the American Automobile Association. And their mode of transportation is shifting: Fewer people are flying or driving this year compared to 2025, and more are traveling by buses, trains and cruises, AAA data shows.

High gas prices and soaring plane ticket costs may factor into the shift. As of Wednesday evening, fuel prices are roughly 17% higher than they were on the same date in 2025, according to AAA data. Meanwhile, "months of elevated jet fuel costs due to the conflict in Iran have contributed to Thanksgiving and Christmas airfares reaching 10-year highs," according to fare-tracking platform Hopper.

The alternate modes of transit may open travelers up to new experiences — and new forms of travel fatigue to keep you from returning home feeling rested and fulfilled. You're probably already familiar with the exhaustion you might get from a day of plane travel, for example. In airplanes, "there can be lower humidity, maybe lower oxygen levels at cabin pressure. Sometimes people report feeling more dehydrated or drained. You're adjusting to that change in altitude," says Alaina Tiani, a Cleveland Clinic behavioral sleep medicine psychologist.

But even waiting in places like train stations or cruise ports can feel draining due to sheer sensory overload, Tiani says. And then, depending on your mode of travel, you may still need to deal with cramped seating and limited ability to get up and walk around or drink some water and eat a snack.

Once you arrive at your destination, managing responsibilities like remembering where you put your hotel key and deciding what to eat and how to structure your day can also take a mental toll, says travel writer Shannon O'Donnell, who's written about managing travel fatigue. "All of that actually requires a lot more thinking and planning for your brain," she says, adding: "People just don't understand how those add up and why a relaxing vacation suddenly has them feeling wrecked."

The consequences can sneak up on you, O'Donnell notes. Travel fatigue can "present as maybe a lack of interest in something that you might usually find fascinating," she says. Instead of looking out the window on a plane ride or playing car games with your kids on a road trip, you might disengage and appear apathetic to the people around you.
Use these tips to manage fatigue, from a travel expert and a sleep specialist
You might stand a better chance of a fulfilling, restful holiday if you prepare for your travel fatigue. Here, Tiani and O'Donnell share their advice for how to do it:

• Come up with a plan before you leave to lighten the load: If you're driving, look up restaurants along your route in advance, says Tiani. Bring snacks with you to places like the airport or train station, O'Donnell suggests. Coming up with a solid itinerary for your trip can help you feel less stressed, Tiani says. She suggests scheduling a rest day in between the day you return home and when you have to get back to your everyday routine.

• Avoid trying to control how the trip will pan out: While planning is useful, rolling with the punches is necessary, too, O'Donnell says. "A lot of travel is being OK with things going wrong, and where you get exhausted is when you try to control more than you can," she says.

• Consider reasonable accommodations: Limit the number of hours you drive in a single day by adding rest stops, or pay for extra legroom on your flight if you'd benefit from it and can afford it, Tiani suggests.

• Prioritize sleep and downtime: Not everyone can comfortably sleep on planes, trains or buses. If you can, get some rest on the way to your destination, Tiani says. During your trip, your sleep routine likely won't be the same because you're in a different setting and operating on a new schedule, she notes.

• Be mindful of your diet: Stay hydrated and aim for balanced meals when you can, Tiani says. O'Donnell agrees: "For train travel and plane travel, that is one of my first sort of defenses: eating well when I get back, loading up on fresh fruits and vegetables, and refueling my body so that it can fight off anything I've been exposed to."

• Move your body: Walking around while traveling, including up and down the corridors of your train or plane when possible, can reduce your risk of blood clots, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Anyone traveling more than four hours by bus, car, train or plane may develop blood clots, according to the agency, though the risk is generally low for the average traveler. Exercise and sunlight exposure are especially useful for dealing with jet lag once you're back home, both Tiani and O'Donnell say.

• Give yourself time to decompress after your trip: After traveling, people may ask you how your travels went. Don't feel bad if you don't want to discuss the whole trip right away, O'Donnell notes. That's a form of travel fatigue itself, she says: "You will look on it differently in two weeks [or] a month's time, just let the guilt go. You don't have to feel any which way about anything. It can be an amazing trip, and also have been really hard."
